In the previous sessions you learned how to manipulate data in R and how to
summarise a single variable: a mean, a variance, a proportion. Each of those
describes **one** quantity at a time.

Today we take the next step: describing how one variable changes **with
another**, and using that relationship to make predictions. This is
**linear regression**, the topic of this week's lecture. By the end of this lab you should be able to

  - fit a simple linear regression model with `lm()`;

  - interpret the intercept and the slope in the units of the problem;

  - compute and interpret residuals, and understand what "least squares" means;

  - measure predictive error and compare a model against a sensible baseline;

  - separate training from test data, and see what overfitting looks like;

  - fit and interpret a model with several predictors, including a categorical one;

  - recognise the standing limits: extrapolation, confounding and sampling
    variability.

As always, you are encouraged to experiment with the code. Change values,
change arguments, and check what happens.

# Part I: a first regression

## The delivery data

We start with the small example used in this week's lecture. A courier company
recorded, for 37 past deliveries, how far the parcel had to travel and how long
the delivery took.

```{r}
deliveries <- data.frame(
  distance_km = c(1, 2, 2.8, 3, 3.2, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5, 6, 7, 7.7, 8, 8.3, 9,
                  10, 10, 10, 10, 11, 11.8, 12, 12.3, 13, 14, 15, 15, 15,
                  15, 16, 17, 17.8, 18, 18.3, 19, 20),
  time_min    = c(15, 13, 19, 18, 14, 16, 17, 19, 20, 22, 23, 20, 27, 27,
                  21, 22, 24, 26, 29, 32, 27, 33, 26, 27, 34, 34, 32, 34,
                  36, 37, 35, 40, 41, 37, 37, 42, 41))

str(deliveries)
```

Each row is one **observation**. The variable we want to predict
(`time_min`) is called the **outcome**, or response; the variable we predict it
from (`distance_km`) is the **predictor**.

Always look at the data before modelling anything.

```{r}
# Notice that this is a "base R plot", i.e., not produced with ggplot2. 
# (OPTIONAL TASK: try reproducing this plot using ggplot2).

plot(time_min ~ distance_km, data = deliveries,
     pch = 16, col = "firebrick", las = 1,
     xlab = "Distance (km)", ylab = "Time (min)",
     main = "37 past deliveries")
```

Notice the two things the lecture emphasised: there is a clear upward pattern,
**and** the points do not lie on a single line. Two deliveries over the same
distance did not take the same time.

## Fitting a line with `lm()`

The function that fits linear models in R is `lm()`. Its first argument is a
**formula**, written `outcome ~ predictor`, and it reads as *"outcome as a function
of predictor"*.

```{r}
# regression of "time_min as a function of distance_km"
fit <- lm(time_min ~ distance_km, data = deliveries)

fit
```

The two numbers printed under `Coefficients` are the estimates $b_0$
(intercept) and $b_1$ (slope) of the fitted line

$$\widehat{\text{Time}} = b_0 + b_1 \times \text{Distance}.$$

You can extract them directly:

```{r}
coef(fit)
```

```{r}
coef(fit)[1]  # intercept, b0
coef(fit)[2]  # slope, b1
```

Rounded, this is $\widehat{\text{Time}} = 12 + 1.5 \times \text{Distance}$ --
the equation used throughout the lecture.

Adding the fitted line to the scatterplot is one line of code:

```{r}
# (OPTIONAL TASK: Try reproducing this plot using ggplot2).

plot(time_min ~ distance_km, data = deliveries,
     pch = 16, col = "firebrick", las = 1,
     xlab = "Distance (km)", ylab = "Time (min)")

abline(fit, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
```

# Part II: residuals and least squares

## Residuals

The model gives a prediction for every delivery we already have. Those
predictions are the **fitted values**, and the gaps between what happened and
what the model said are the **residuals**:

$$e_i = Y_i - \hat{Y}_i.$$

R gives you both.

```{r}
head(fitted(fit))     # the predicted times
head(residuals(fit))  # observed minus predicted
```

It is worth seeing the residuals as the vertical gaps they are.

```{r}
# This is a slightly trickier plot to reproduce in ggplot2.
# You can try it if you're feeling confident, but don't let yourself get stuck 
# here -- complete the lab, then come back to practice your ggplot2 skills if 
# you'd like.

plot(time_min ~ distance_km, data = deliveries,
     pch = 16, col = "firebrick", las = 1,
     xlab = "Distance (km)", ylab = "Time (min)")

abline(fit, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)

# one vertical segment per observation, from the point to the line
segments(x0 = deliveries$distance_km, y0 = deliveries$time_min,
         x1 = deliveries$distance_km, y1 = fitted(fit),
         col = "firebrick")
```

A **positive** residual means the delivery took longer than the model
predicted; a negative one means it was quicker.

## What makes a line "best"?

The lecture compared three candidate lines through the same cloud of points.
Let us write a small function that scores any line by its **sum of squared
residuals**, and use it to compare them.

```{r}
ssr <- function(b0, b1, data = deliveries){
  predicted <- b0 + b1 * data$distance_km
  residuals <- data$time_min - predicted
  return(sum(residuals ^ 2))
}
```

```{r}
ssr(12, 1.5)    # the regression line
ssr(19, 1.5)    # right slope, but 7 minutes too high
ssr(27.5, 0)    # a horizontal line at the mean delivery time
```

The three lines, drawn together:

```{r}
# Note that even base R plots can be quite rich in terms of information.
# Not everything needs to be a ggplot2 :)

plot(time_min ~ distance_km, data = deliveries,
     pch = 16, col = "firebrick", las = 1,
     xlab = "Distance (km)", ylab = "Time (min)")

abline(a = 12,   b = 1.5, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
abline(a = 19,   b = 1.5, col = "grey40",    lwd = 2, lty = 2)
abline(a = 27.5, b = 0,   col = "grey40",    lwd = 2, lty = 3)

legend("topleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.8,
       legend = c("regression line", "too high", "horizontal at the mean"),
       col = c("steelblue", "grey40", "grey40"),
       lty = c(1, 2, 3), lwd = 2)
```

# Part III: how good is the model?

## A larger dataset

The delivery data are small and tidy, which makes them good for a first look.
From here on we return to the `penguins` dataset you met last week, and ask
whether a penguin's **body mass** can be predicted from its **flipper length**.

As before, we remove the observations with missing values.

```{r}
# library(palmerpenguins) # <-- load this if not already loaded
penguins_clean <- penguins %>%
  filter(!is.na(body_mass_g), !is.na(flipper_length_mm), !is.na(sex))

nrow(penguins_clean)
```

```{r}
# Another base R scatterplot. 
plot(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm, data = penguins_clean,
     pch = 16, col = "firebrick", las = 1,
     xlab = "Flipper length (mm)", ylab = "Body mass (g)")
```

```{r}
# Simple linear regression
pfit <- lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm, data = penguins_clean)

coef(pfit)
```

## Measuring prediction error

As in the lecture, we summarise how far the predictions fall from the
observations by the **average error**, the average length of the residuals:

$$
\text{Average error}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lvert Y_i-\hat{Y}_i\rvert .
$$

It is in the units of the outcome (here grams), which makes it easy to talk
about. In software and in many books it is called the *mean absolute error*
(MAE). The absolute value is essential: without it the positive and negative
residuals would cancel, and for a least-squares line with an intercept they
cancel exactly.

We will need the average error several times, so we write a small function
for it.

```{r}
avg_error <- function(y, y_hat) mean(abs(y - y_hat))

e <- residuals(pfit)

model_error <- avg_error(penguins_clean$body_mass_g, fitted(pfit))

model_error
```

An error of a few hundred grams means nothing on its own. **Compared with what?** 
he simplest possible baseline model would be one that ignores flipper length 
entirely and predicts the mean body mass for every penguin.

```{r}
baseline_pred <- mean(penguins_clean$body_mass_g)
baseline_e    <- penguins_clean$body_mass_g - baseline_pred

baseline_error <- avg_error(penguins_clean$body_mass_g, baseline_pred)

c(baseline = baseline_error, model = model_error)
```

## $R^2$

$R^2$ makes that same comparison with squared errors, on a 0–1 scale:

$$
R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum (Y_i-\hat{Y}_i)^2}{\sum (Y_i-\bar{Y})^2}.
$$

It is generally easy to compute it, even if we do it "the long way" -- especially 
if you notice that the denominator is the sum of squared errors on the fitted 
regression, and the denominator is the sum of squared regressions on the 
"predict everything as the mean" baseline.

```{r}
r2_manual <- 1 - sum(e ^ 2) / sum(baseline_e ^ 2)

r2_manual
```

```{r}
summary(pfit)$r.squared
```

The `summary()` of a fitted model contains a great deal more:

```{r}
summary(pfit)
```

You are not expected to interpret all of this yet: 
  - you have already met standard errors (recall that they are the standard 
  deviation of the sampling  distribution of an estimator -- yes, the regression 
  coefficients are *sample estimates*! We'll look more into that later).
  - $p$-values will come later in the module, when we discuss hypothesis testing.

For now, locate the two coefficients, the `Residual standard error` and the 
`Multiple R-squared`.

### Going further (optional): the RMSE

The lecture uses only the average error, but software usually also reports the
**root mean squared error**,

$$
\mathrm{RMSE}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i-\hat{Y}_i)^2}
=\sqrt{\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{res}}/n}.
$$

It is also in grams, but because it squares before averaging it penalises the
large misses more heavily. It is never smaller than the average error, and the
gap between the two widens as the errors become more uneven. The baseline's
RMSE is $\sqrt{\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{total}}/n}$, so the ratio of the two RMSEs
is exactly $\sqrt{1-R^2}$. The `Residual standard error` in `summary(pfit)` is
nearly the same quantity, $\sqrt{\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{res}}/(n-2)}$: it divides
by $n-2$ instead of $n$.

```{r}
c(average_error = model_error,
  RMSE          = sqrt(mean(e ^ 2)),
  residual_SE   = sigma(pfit))
```

# Part IV: training and test data

An error computed on the same observations used to fit the model is optimistic:
the model was chosen to suit exactly those points. The honest question is how
it performs on penguins it has never seen.

Let's split the data into a **training set** and a **test set**.

```{r}
set.seed(2024)   # so that everyone in the lab gets the same split

n     <- nrow(penguins_clean)
train_id <- sample(seq_len(n), size = round(0.7 * n))

train <- penguins_clean[train_id, ]
test  <- penguins_clean[-train_id, ]

c(n_train = nrow(train), n_test = nrow(test))
```

We fit on the training set **only**, then predict the test set.

```{r}
fit_train <- lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm, data = train)

pred_test <- predict(fit_train, newdata = test)

train_error <- avg_error(train$body_mass_g, fitted(fit_train))
test_error  <- avg_error(test$body_mass_g,  pred_test)

c(train = train_error, test = test_error)
```

These are the two numbers of the lecture's *Training and test data* slide: the
average error on the penguins used to fit the line, and on the held-out ones.
For a model this simple they are usually close: a straight line has very little
capacity to chase noise.

> **NOTE**: This is possibly the most basic concept in statistical modelling and 
machine learning: you don't test your model on the same data that was used to 
develop it. It sounds simple (and it often is), but it can be sometimes 
subtle -- especially when 
aggregating data from different sources (which may or may not be independen) or 
working with data that has some sort of grouping structure. We'll discuss this 
further in future weeks.

# Part V: more than one predictor

Flipper length is not the only thing that varies between these penguins. The
three species differ in size, and within a species males tend to be heavier
than females. Multiple regression lets us use several predictors at once,

$$
\hat{Y}=b_0+b_1X_1+b_2X_2+\cdots+b_pX_p,
$$

and R's formula interface adds predictors with `+`.

```{r}
mfit <- lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm + species, data = penguins_clean)

coef(mfit)
```

Notice what happened to `species`. It is a **factor** with three levels, and R
has represented it by comparing each level with a **reference category** — the
first level, `Adelie`. The coefficient `speciesGentoo` is therefore read as
*"the difference in predicted body mass between a Gentoo and an Adelie penguin
of the same flipper length"*.

```{r}
levels(penguins_clean$species)
```

# Part VI: limits and uncertainty

## Extrapolation

A fitted model will happily return a number for any input you give it, whether
or not the data support it.

```{r}
range(penguins_clean$flipper_length_mm)
```

```{r}
predict(pfit, newdata = data.frame(flipper_length_mm = c(200, 260, 400)))
```

**Answer**:

## The fitted line is an estimate too

Our coefficients came from one sample of penguins. A different sample would
give different coefficients. We can see that directly, using exactly the
resampling idea from last week's lab.
    
```{r}
set.seed(2024)
slopes <- map_dbl(1:500, \(i){
  s <- penguins_clean %>% slice_sample(n = 50)
  coef(lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm, data = s))[2]
})
hist(slopes, breaks = 25, col = "lightblue", las = 1,
     main = "Sampling distribution of the slope (n = 50)",
     xlab = "Estimated slope (g per mm)")

sd(slopes)
```

That histogram is the **sampling distribution** of the slope, and its spread is
the **standard error** of the slope — the same quantity R printed in the
`summary()` output above, in the column headed `Std. Error`.

## Where this goes next
                  
Everything in this lab predicted a **number**: minutes, or grams. Next week we
keep the same machinery — a predictor, coefficients to interpret, a criterion
to fit, a baseline to beat, a held-out check — but change the outcome to a
**label**: was the delivery late, yes or no? That is logistic regression.
